utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that you, Mr. Mikulicic, would like to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it's me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had Markac Defence, but Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Along the lines of the discussions that we had yesterday regarding statements, interviews and methodology, I wanted to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention two other references. We saw the reference yesterday to Mr. Jarnjak's interview. The first reference is transcript dated December 12th of 2008. Mr. Cayley and I both raised this issue. The transcript number -- page references are 13.631, beginning at line 6, going to 13.634, going to line 13. And I would note, specifically your comments, Mr. President, in this particular colloquy that went on regarding the use -- or regarding the methodology of interviews where you said, and I can't specifically -- don't have the line because I printed it out on my e-mail: "And you would say you would not add the kind of things the investigator added when he did put the questions to the witness at that time, which I would not have taught him if I ever would have given a course of examination of potential witnesses." The second reference is Witness Zganjer, and that was November 12th of 2008, beginning on page 11.603. And there was question and answer regarding investigation methodology at line 15, and the question Mr. Mikulicic asks at line 15 as part of the question is: "He," meaning the investigator, "characterised them in the following way: That the interviews conducted were very poor, that they were not compiled in any sort of format, that the contents of these interviews did not really make a contribution or bring anything in, and that you should not perceive this as criticism leveled against you," meaning the investigator was telling this to Mr. Zganjer. So I just wanted to add that, Your Honours, to the discussion that occurred yesterday with specific references to witnesses, dates and transcripts. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I guess this would be a good opportunity, then, with respect to the Jarnjak interview that was shown to the Chamber yesterday, we would like that admitted but not for -- as substantive evidence and not for the truth of the matters asserted in the discussion but, rather, as indicative of methodology and techniques used in those situations, and the probative value being that -- as I have read the Limaj and Popovic decisions referenced on Friday by the Chamber, one of the factors in considering whether to admit Mr. Pasic's 2002 statement concerning the matters which he subsequently changed, but to admit those changed portions as substantive evidence, one of the factors that the Limaj and Popovic Chambers considered was the fact that the Chamber could examine the methodology used in the questioning, because both -- in both circumstances, I believe, the interviews were videotaped. And if in fact the methodology of the 2002 statement is going to be a factor in consideration of admission, then we would submit that the Jarnjak video is probative with respect to methodology and, therefore, we would move to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the -- the probative value of the interview of Mr. Jarnjak is so low in respect of this witness that doesn't meet the threshold for admissibility. It's clear from the witness's answers yesterday that the witness did -- that the interview was conducted in a different manner with him than it was with Mr. Jarnjak, who was interviewed as a suspect. And in particular, the witness made it clear that there was no suggestion that he was involved in any wrong-doing, no suggestion that the witness was involved in any planning or that others were involved in any planning that the witness may not have been involved in, and in light of the different types of interviews and the different way the interviews were conducted, I don't think the Jarnjak interview has a sufficient probative value in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe the Prosecution's argument goes to weight. Obviously we have different arguments. The witness also said that he felt the questions were suggestive and leading, and felt that -- he did not feel comfortable in resisting the suggestions posed to him. Nevertheless, this is argument between the Prosecution and the Defence. We submit that it can be argued at a later date, but with respect to probative value, I believe the Jarnjak video in addition to what Mr. Kuzmanovic raised this morning, which is the Zganjer situation, and I believe it was Witness Turkalj, where the Chamber itself expressed concerns about the techniques used by Mr. Foster, establishes a pattern and that pattern may very well be relevant to the Chamber in its evaluation of whether to admit the portions of the 2002 Pasic statement which at issue here. We would suggest under Rule 89 that it certainly has probative value and there's no reason that it should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, brief, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mr. Misetic is suggesting that the Jarnjak interview is relevant to the assessment of the evidence of Mr. Zganjer or Mr. Turkalj; if he is, those interviewed were actually admitted and the Chamber can see them, and there's no need to compare them with any other interview. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I just clarify, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think you tendered the interview in evidence. Ms. Gustafson responded. You had an opportunity to further explain, and now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: She's asking whether I'm suggesting something. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is sufficiently informed. Mr. Misetic, has the relevant portion of the interview been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I yesterday expressed some concern as where the beginning it says, This is what we say and it seems that that's what you are saying, which there's at least a suggestion that there has been something prior to that, which is then summarised. I do not know whether that is true or not. But I would like to know -- Ms. Gustafson, have you considered whether there are any other portions which, if this video would be admitted into evidence, which you would like to have added for context?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did look at it yesterday, but I would need a little more time to determine exactly which pages. If I could get back to the Chamber on that, if the Chamber is inclined to admit this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for two reasons, the uploaded video will be MFI'd. The first reason being that the Chamber will have to consider whether or not the probative value is such as argued by Ms. Gustafson, that it's fit to be admitted. The second one to give Ms. Gustafson some time to see whether there's any additional portion that should be added for purposes of context. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me just -- if I can assist the Registrar. It's 65 ter 1D2988.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1719, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any other matter to be raised? If not, I think we were at a point that the Chamber had looked at the video, has put some questions, and that you still would like to continue your re-cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will continue to hear your evidence, but I would like to remind you first that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony last week. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, again, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start off this morning by asking you a question following up on a question asked of you by the Prosecutor. You will recall yesterday you were read portions from a report by the Special Rapporteur concerning an allegation that people were being prevented from coming back into Croatia, and you were asked whether had you any reason to question the observations of the Special Rapporteur. And I'd like to call your attention, again, to Exhibit P822, and that is the exhibit where the European Union Monitoring Mission reports, on the 27th and 28th of October, on a meeting with you where you said that 100 Serbs had in fact returned from Serbia by October 27th and that the European Union mission suggests in its report that that is accurate. And the report specifically says: "Indeed, some people are returning." If you look there at paragraph 2(a), the specific quote is: "According to Mr. Pasic, more than 100 have returned from Serbia. The number growing every day." Then there's a comment: "Indeed, some people are returning, but only those with property secured. Team still wait to see when an actual occupant of a house is driven out because the legal owner returns." My question to you is: If in fact there were obstacles at the border so that people couldn't return, how did these 100 Serbs get back into the Knin area from Serbia by the 27th of October?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I did not sense any obstacle for the return of those Serbs who had fled to return to the Republic of Croatia. I specifically say that because the Croatian government enabled those Serbs who were in the Republic of Serbia to receive Croatian documents as proof of their Croatian nationality, in Beli Manastir and Vukovar, and many of them used that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These 100 or so Serbs that had returned by the 27th of October, do you know what kind of papers - meaning passports, citizenship, et cetera - they had which allowed them to cross back into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some received their Croatian papers immediately, while other, as far as I know, came with certain refugee IDs which had been issued to them in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who -- which governmental authority issued these refugee IDs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was issued by the Republic of Serbia, although I don't know which authority. It may have been the UNHCR or someone else. I have to say, though, that a number of Serbs who came back, came back in an organised fashion on a bus with the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn your attention next to Exhibit P2648, which is Mr. Al-Alfi's report of a meeting with you in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now -- yes, if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, throughout this report, he refers to you as the mayor. Do you know why he's referring to you as the mayor?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was probably not familiar with the term "governmental commissioner."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is more than two months after your first appearance in Knin and after several meetings -- at least -- I should correct that. After at least one other meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi that we've seen. Did you not, at any opportunity, explain to him that you're not the mayor but the governmental commissioner for an area wider than simply the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did not. I didn't meet him on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 5 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is -- you were asked some questions about comments made by Mr. Kostovic that are referenced in paragraph 5. What comments did Mr. Kostovic make?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, Mr. Kostovic, as deputy prime minister, advocated the possibility of a further stay of the remaining Serbian population after Operation Storm. He was probably reacting to a separate UN envoy report and that of Ms. Elisabeth Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what it is that Mr. Al-Alfi could have believed was -- strike that question. Let me ask you about paragraph 7 of this document. There's -- he's reporting on a discussion concerning the fact that you may be changed very soon. Are you familiar with the constitutional law on ethnic minorities which was in effect into September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially I was. That law was in force, and as far as I know, parts of it were being implemented; whereas, others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that, in fact, that law required that, pursuant to the 1991 census, the government's commissioner for the Knin area had to be an ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not necessarily have to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, what about the chiefs of the Kotar-Knin police administration, or the police station in Knin, did they have to be ethnic Serbs under the law?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs, but I'm not familiar with whether the persons in such positions had to be Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn your attention to a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is P2647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the last two questions raise an issue as to the knowledge of this witness of the legislation under which he functioned. I have no clear recollection, as a matter of fact, to the text of this legislation, so in order to be able to assess, could you tell us, I take it that these documents are -- this legislation is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could perhaps assist the Chamber, if you would know. Otherwise we will try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head but I have asked my Case Manager to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were shown a series of documents yesterday concerning people that applied to you or General Cermak seeking to live in Knin. If we look at the first three names or four names, I guess, on this document, which of these people, if any, were refugees from the area that were living outside of the area at the time this letter was written?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the list, when I look at their last names, it is perhaps only the Vujic person who may have come from Kijevo, originally; whereas, the others did not hail from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were they refugees perhaps from other areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe. Personally I never met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Some of the other documents in this group also discuss companies wanting to move in to the area and having housing for their workers. Is that something that was common at the time, that, if companies moved into the area, that they would ask to you provide housing for workers that may be coming in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That possibility did exist and it was used. I have to say, in particular, that this was the case with the Croatian railways, as well as with the various institutions of state authority; that is to say, the judiciary, the educational system, the police, and a letter of that kind arrived from a former factory called Sintal, which is in Oklaj. The municipal head in Promina, whose name, I believe, was Zeljko Dzapo [phoen], asked that housing units be secured for about one or 200 workers who were supposed to initiate the production process within the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, am I correct that you were actually a member of the housing commission that was established after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was. My legal affairs assistant, Slavko Djakovic, was. Another commission member was Silvana Dumancic, who was also a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the work of the housing commission, however, in that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was the housing commission charged with making decisions as to which houses could be used to house refugees pursuant to the Law on Temporary Take Over of Property?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these decisions, how many people were on the commission, the housing commission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The housing commission was defined by a law. The housing commission was composed of the representatives of the commissioner's office of the government of the Croatia, members of the secretary or, rather, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Defence, the Centre for Social Welfare, and I believe that there was also a representative of the Red Cross. I may have left somebody out, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the work of this housing commission, based on your knowledge of its work, was there a policy of trying to take away homes from Serbs, that you were aware of, and to re-populate their homes with Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Law on Temporary Use of Property owned by displaced or refugeed Serbs was promulgated, that applied to both apartments and houses. I don't have a feeling, I didn't have a feeling then, I don't have it now, that the politicians had any intention of moving in people from a certain area, in larger numbers. Most people came of their own will, spontaneously. And I said yesterday that some of them had to arrive, because when the Serbs left Knin, in Banja Luka and some other cities, the Croats were chased away by them, and they moved into their houses with the words, You have my house, or my apartment, in the place where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the answer to your question that you posed about the law is -- it's Exhibit D836 and an amendment is at D900.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to go back now to your 2002 statement, and I'm going to ask you a few questions for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1706.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm referencing the portion that we've discussed many times, which is -- that there's a portion in there that says that you believe the looting and destruction that took place was planned from above. And I know that you've said that you, in fact, did not say that, but let me just ask you a few questions. Did you ever attend any meetings of -- well, let me ask it -- a first question. What do you understand when -- when someone were -- if someone were to say "the top of the government"? What is "the top," in your view?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The top of the government" would be the president of the Republic, prime minister, and all the government ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How many meetings did you attend with the president, the prime minister, or the government ministers prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to Operation Storm, I did not attend a single meeting with the prime minister; I attended a few meetings with Mr. Mate Granic, but that was in 1993 or 1994. In any case, prior to Operation Storm. I also attended one or two meetings with Mr. Ramljak, who, during the course of Operation Storm, was no longer a deputy prime minister ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your discussions with Mr. Granic or Mr. Ramljak, did you ever get any impression that there was a plan to allow looting and destruction to take place if, in fact, Croatia ever retook the so-called Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And if you will allow me, I would like to clarify a situation. It concerns my meeting with Mr. Granic. In 1993, humanitarian aid was sent to the Croats who resided in Knin. That aid went through a Zagreb-based company called Unikonzum. He insisted, when it came to the settlements of Potkonje and Nunic, which was still -- which were still inhabited by both Croats and Serbs, he insisted on the reciprocity of sending humanitarian aid. For example, in -- if there were 50 Croats in Nunic, he insisted, and that's the only way humanitarian aid could be sent if humanitarian and -- aid was sent for 50 Serbs, although there may have been more of them living in the area at the time. But the point that I'm driving home with this illustrations is the fact that the reciprocity in providing humanitarian aid to the area was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what orders were issued within the Ministry of the Interior prior to Operation Storm concerning policing in the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any orders that were issued within the Croatian Army prior to Operation Storm concerning prevention of crime in the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Speaking generally, do you have any specific basis to know, based on documents, conversations, or meetings that you attended, what the Croatian -- the top of the Croatian leadership intended with respect to crime, whether crime commission or crime prevention, in the newly liberated areas, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph on page 8, which is on B/C/S page 12 of your statement, after the sentence that says, "I believe that the looting and destruction that took place was planned from above," it says: "It was anarchy in Knin. Only the president could have stopped it. Despite my suggestion to Cermak at one of the meetings that it wouldn't look good if the president saw all the destruction and burning, it was still continuing when he came to Knin." My question -- and again, Mr. Pasic, I understand your position today with respect to this paragraph, but I need to ask you this question anyway. Can you explain the logic in this paragraph because the beginning of the paragraph says the looting and destruction you believe was planned from above, you've explained that "above" would have included the president. Then it says: "Only the president could have stopped it," and that you said, "... it wouldn't look good if the president saw all the destruction and burning." So my -- I -- can you help me reconcile how, on the one hand, sentence 1 suggests that President Tudjman would have been involved in planning the destruction and burning; and sentence 3 says that you didn't think it would be a -- it would be good for the president to see the destruction and burning? I'm not sure I understand the logic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logic is clear. I believe that I did say that the president couldn't. However, I believe that this is a mistake. That's why it says only the president could have prevented. The president could not have prevented anything. I confirm that the situation was tantamount to partial anarchy, and in one conversation with Mr. Cermak, I said it wouldn't be good for the president of the Republic to see smoke and fire burning -- fires burning around Knin, as he was addressing the citizens of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about sentence 2, about whether the president could or couldn't have stopped it. This goes more to what actually took place at the interview in 2002, if can you recall this specific portion of the discussion you had with Mr. Foster, okay? How can it be that -- can you explain who said what, because sentence 1 suggests that President Tudjman would have been involved in planning the looting and destruction. Sentence 3 of the same paragraph has you saying that it wouldn't look good if the president saw all the destruction and burning. So who said what in the -- can you recall how this paragraph got into your statement, and can you reconcile the first sentence with the third sentence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this was recorded, but I can't reconcile one with the other. They contradict each other. If the president could prevent looting or arson, and he didn't, because he never planned it, I would not have stated that it wouldn't be good for the president to see the destruction and arson or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going to page 4 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is B/C/S page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the last answers are puzzling me. You said -- let me just ... It is on the basis of contradiction that you said that you confirmed, if I understand you well, that, during the interview, you said that it would -- wouldn't be good for the president to see the destruction and arson or any such thing. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- you were referring to a certain conversation with Mr. Cermak. Do you remember at what point in time was it when the president would come to the area; and, if so, what visit was planned which made you say this to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had several conversations with Mr. Cermak about the situation in the liberated area. We both expressed our dissatisfaction with some of the security issues. I believe that this was on the eve of the president's arrival on the train, when he was to stop in Knin on -- on his way from Zagreb to Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that wouldn't be good for him to see all that. Was there any way to prevent him from seeing smoke and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was very difficult to prevent. He could not see smoke, but the question was how to prevent the burning of the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say there was no smoke but would -- you had to prevent any burning so that the president would not be confronted with any smoke and that he -- therefore, the situation should be such that there was not even smoke to be seen when he would travel on this train through the area. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do not understand it that way. I thought that it would be good for the president not to see any smoke, and also that there was no arson. He may have seen cases of arson, as he was travelling on -- on -- by train from Zagreb to Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand, then, what you are saying. You say, It would be good for him not to see it. At the same time, you say there may have been smoke, so he would see it, unless -- I have difficulties in understanding exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it should be difficult. When I said that the president -- that it wouldn't be good for the president to see smoke, what I meant was that it would actually be good if there had been no arson or smoke, irrespective of the president's presence or anybody else's presence in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there was smoke and arson; so, therefore, of course, it would be good if he wouldn't see it. But since it was there, just looking out of the window would have -- so I'm trying to understand the gist of this remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of this is the fact that I said that it would be good for the president not to see smoke and fire. This also leads to something else, and that other thing is that it should -- it would be good to stop and prevent the burning of abandoned properties and houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was a need to stop it and to further prevent the burning of abandoned property and houses, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow up, Mr. Pasic. Did you think that President Tudjman would be angry if he saw fire and smoke?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I supposed that he would have been dissatisfied if he knew what the real situation on the ground was, if he learned what the situation on the ground was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you -- I want to make sure that we're talking about what you supposed, in August 1995, when you said at the time that it wouldn't be good -- it wouldn't look good if the president saw all the destruction and burning. What did -- how did you think the president -- at the time, in August 1995, how did you think the president would react if he saw all the destruction and burning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he would have expressed his dissatisfaction. I believe that he would go through the government of the Republic, or through the ministries to react, in order to have the situation improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say that the president would have reacted through the ministries in order to have the situation improve, did you think at that time that the president could have called for new people to be brought in to -- to get the situation under control?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was him but it was somebody else who did that, and what was done was that, after that, I don't know when, not immediately after the freedom train passed through Knin, the number of the members of the Ministry of the Interior in the territory of the city of Knin was increased, or, rather, in the territory that fell under the jurisdiction of the commissioner of the government of the Republic of Croatia for Knin. And also the police forces were replenished partly with officers from the county of Primorje and Gorski Kotar, and I believe that members of the Croatian MUP arrived from Varazdin county as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to wrap up this issue to go back to what my original question was about this paragraph. If, in fact, I think in August of 1995, you were concerned that the president would be dissatisfied by what he saw on the ground, then, can you make any sense of the sentence in that paragraph that suggests that in fact President Tudjman would have been involved in planning those crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you finished with this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do I have to understand your testimony that if President Tudjman would not have seen the smoke with his own eyes, he would have been unaware of what happened on the ground, that he not have known about the burning and that it was through his personal observation that he would learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, shouldn't there really be some foundation for that, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he said it would not be good if he would see it, and -- let me, Mr. -- from the follow-up questions, you'll -- Could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The president did not have to come to Knin personally or pass through Knin in order to become aware of the situation. He had a lot of other ways at his disposal to get informed about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether he would see the smoke at that moment or not would not really change his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would not have changed anything. He could have obtained information in other ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So seeing the smoke would not have caused his dissatisfaction because it did not add substantially to his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how he would have felt, but if his feelings were like mine, then he would not have felt comfortable with what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Irrespective of what he saw, because you said that he would have other means to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I start from the president's letter, which was published a few days or maybe on the eve of Operation Storm. In that letter, he invited and appealed to the citizens of the Serb ethnicity who were Croatian citizens to remain in his homes [as interpreted], that peace and normal life was guaranteed to them. I believe that this shows that the president of the Republic did not have any intention of causing the events to evolve in the way they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you gained the impression that more people were sent to Knin after the visit of the president, which suggests that you considered his personal observation to be a factor in sending more people to Knin. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I put it quite the same way. And if I did, that's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell me -- I'll try to find ... You said you believed that he would go through the government of the Republic or through the ministries to react, in order to have the situation improved. And this, on the basis of an expression of dissatisfaction after he would have seen the smoke. That's at least how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I presume that the president of the Republic on that day did not even see smoke. Perhaps there may have been arson elsewhere, sufficiently far away for him not to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what is that presumption based, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which one? The last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you presumed that the president on that day did not even see smoke. Are you talking about the Knin area or just the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he did not see drills of smoke, then I had in mind the area of the town of Knin and along the railroad that goes further on to Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you not expect the president to see any smoke close to the railway on which he was travelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He may have, and then he may have not seen any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any recent burning of houses close to the railway on the day the freedom train travelled through the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then specifically ask you whether you think that burning of houses in Grubori, just before the arrival of the freedom train, would have been visible from that train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no way that one could see Grubori from the train or from any railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the smoke from Grubori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With difficulty, because the distance is at least 10 kilometres, and the lie of land is such that it makes it impossible for one to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, what sources of information did President Tudjman have about burning and looting, specifically?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what information he had. I did not send him any information. I don't know who else could have warned the republican president of the events in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then can I ask you: How do you know what the president knew or didn't know before he took the freedom train to Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he knew before he boarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is specifically, in your statement, with respect to this conversation where you said you told General Cermak that it wouldn't look good if the president saw all the destruction and burning, at that time, was it your belief that the president would be better informed once he got to Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then what would it matter if the president saw all the destruction and burning? Why would you tell General Cermak it wouldn't look good if the president saw it? If he already knows it, then who cares if the president saw it or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say now why I said that. I felt the need to say that it would not have been good for the president of the Republic to see that, irrespective of the fact that it was likely, that through, other sources, he could have been informed of the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, Mr. Pasic, let me just put it to you, you didn't want the president to see it because you were concerned that he would have a negative reaction to seeing burning, and that's why you mentioned that to General Cermak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 4 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say, for example, you would send reports -- you talk about your relationship to Mr. Mijic and Mr. Romanic. You say you had a good relationship with Mr. Mijic. "I would personally send reports to Milos Mihic and Romanic, and after they had gone to Zvonko Gambiroza, about citizens who were abused and when crimes were reported to me. But nothing was done about them." And then in the next paragraph: "The police coordinators who were sent down from the ministry were in control of the police. That's why they were sent down. Either they couldn't or wouldn't do anything about the looting, or perhaps they had been told to keep their eyes closed." Now, what is the basis -- I know, again, we keep in mind your clarifications and corrections, so I'm aware of them, Mr. Pasic. But would you have had any reason to know what a police coordinator was or wasn't told to do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "coordinator" means that they had to -- a consultative role in the work of the police in the town of Knin and the district of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in light of your good relationship with Mr. Mijic, who is the police chief of the Knin police, and your relationship with Mr. Romanic, who is the chief of police of the entire Kotar, did they ever tell you that they had been told to keep their eyes closed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to crimes that you reported to them, did they ever tell you whether they were doing something about the crimes that you were reporting to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they said that it was also clear from certain earlier reports that a number of perpetrators were brought in and interrogated. I don't know how the rest of that procedure developed though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Mijic and Mr. Romanic had encountered some sort of pressure not to investigate or prevent crime -- well, let me ask the first question. Did they ever tell you that they had received any kind of pressure to either not investigate crime that took place or not to prevent crime that might take place in the future?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussions with them as to why they were having problems with the security situation on the ground? Was there -- do you recall any conversations where they said, We're having trouble because of a certain reason or reasons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did discuss those issues with them. The conclusion was always that the area was very large with a great number of settlements, as well as with many access roads, and, at the same time, that they had too few policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When did these discussions take place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently. We would speak in the morning, then during the meetings called by them or by myself, or if we ever met in the field or in the town itself. We would always be discussing those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next issue is on the role of the military commanders. Do you recall at any time through August or September 1995 that anyone said at any of these meetings that you attended that, The problem is we need to get in touch with General Gotovina to have him solve these problems?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest going to General Cervenko or President Tudjman to ask that something be done along the military line?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If, in fact, the problems in the area were perceived to be because the command line wasn't functioning, do you think that someone, at some point, would have said, We need it get in touch with someone at the top of the command line to see if they can fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert to be able to assess the hierarchy and the chain of command and whether it functioned disjointedly. The chain of command is simply not an area in which I can discuss matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, at page 8 of your statement in English, which is page 12 in the B/C/S, there's a sentence attributed to you that says: "I was hoping that I would be able to help both Croats and Serbs, but that was made impossible by the policies and those in power." Now, you've spoken about President Tudjman. You've spoken about General Cermak, Mr. Mihic, Mr. Romanic and yourself. Who would have been in power to make it impossible to help both Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was such a force which, at that moment, could have helped either one group or the other. Throughout the war, I followed the plight of both peoples. At first, I followed the plight of expelled Croats who had been driven out of Knin by my compatriots, the Serbs. After that, it was difficult for me to watch and follow the plight of my ethnic community, which was significantly reduced in the area. Many of that group simply left. It was -- happened because when the Serbs were destroying the property of Croats, they were also destroying parts of themselves. They failed to understand that, by burning, killing and expelling, they may have caused a turn of events which would be directed at them some day. They did not realise that the property was a part of the state, irrespective of the fact whether the owner was a Croat or a Serb. If I may, while we're on the topic of prevention, I would say that it was difficult to rein in a person, whether that person belonged to the Croatian Army, the military, or if he was just an ordinary citizen. If, after five years of expulsion, he returned to his home, and upon his return, he came across a pile of stone out of which a fig tree rose, who could have stopped such a person to repeat those actions, which have caused his plight initially? I simply cannot say anything to try and defend such behaviour. I condemn it, but I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pasic, while we are on that page, I did want to ask you, if you could just explain one event on this page. There's three paragraphs beneath the paragraph we were just looking at. It says: "I remember that I was with my deputy on one occasion when we caught a military policeman stealing equipment from a factory. We took him to the military police but nothing happened." Do you recall such an incident, and, if so, can you explain how you and your deputy could have, what appears to be, arrested a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My deputy or my assistant was Ivan Barisic. He was an engineer, and before the war, before he had been expelled from Knin, he worked in the screw factory there. We went to the tool work-shop of the factory, since he was interested in it at the time. I wasn't very familiar with that facility, but we came across a member of the Croatian military police. This remains etched in my memory. I think his name was either Baturina or Badurina, and together with him we went to see Mr. Orsulic. We reported his behaviour. I don't know what the consequences were, but I could see at the time that he was simply taking away stuff he would never need. I don't know what followed though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The statement says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I notice that on your previous question there was a long answer which had hardly to do anything with your question. Are you -- do you want an answer or are you just satisfied that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tells us a lot of things but without giving an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought he did give me an answer to the question, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he gave an answer -- well. You asked him about the policies and those in power. I didn't hear anything about policies and power, but, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wide story -- well, I do not know. if you consider that your question has been answered, then, of course, I'd leave to that. I just observed that I didn't gain the impression that I heard an answer to what I understood to be your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, then, let's go back to that question. Do you know of anyone specifically who was in power who was trying to prevent you from being able to help Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know or recall how that statement got into your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say it, Mr. Pasic, or didn't you say that, either confirming a question, or is it just invented by those who interviewed you? Or did you say a thing of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I said anything of the sort. Something like that could not have happened, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, perhaps always, if we are referring to his statement, we first verify whether the witness thinks that this is something of the sort he said, because, to explore the further basis, if he wouldn't have said that, doesn't make much sense. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, with respect to the issue of the military policeman that you referred to Mr. Orsulic, it says: "We took him to the military police but nothing happened." That's at least what it says in the English. Did you physically take this military policeman to the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went there with us. Neither me nor Mr. Barisic needed to use any force, and I couldn't order him to follow us. Simply as if nothing had happened, he accompanied us. He didn't take anything on that occasion, because we prevented him. And after that, I simply don't know what happened. I didn't have any contact with Mr. Orsulic about that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you came upon him, you -- he wanted to steal things but you prevented it; and then he voluntarily walked with you to the military police command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I just have two short areas to cover with you. The first is, I'd like to show you a video and ask that you confirm the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D2981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it is referred -- you referred to this in your statement but this is the actual video of your call to the Serbian population on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's broadcast on Croatian state television.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Petar Pasic is going to have a lot of work to do soon. He's the Croatian government commissioner for Knin. "Petar Pasic: I would like to convey my sincere congratulations to the leadership on bringing the decision to undertake a decisive military police action with the aim of reintegrating the occupied areas and reaching the internationally recognised borders of the Republic of Croatia. I would also like to congratulate all those who participated in the brilliantly conducted action. I expect that Croatia and its military police and police forces, as well as current government, will demonstrate all of their democratic strength and will in these historic times, which will be crucial particularly for the citizens, for Croatian citizens of Serb nationality, to remain in their homes as loyal citizens to whom the state of Croatia will guarantee all constitutional rights belonging to them. "I appeal to you once again, stay. Remain calm and wait for the Croatian authority. Today is the day of your victory."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, is that the statement that you read out on Croatian state television on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances, how it came about that you were allowed to appeal to the Croatian citizens of Serb nationality to say in their homes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't understand how these questions arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was -- understood that I had a little leeway in my re-cross, and this would have been something that I'm using with respect to the 2002 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The letter was tendered by Mr. Kay and there's no -- this letter and this subject isn't addressed by the witness in any of his corrections, so I'm not sure it relates to the leeway that Mr. Misetic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think that was given to you at a certain context, that is, that you would not have to cross-examine the witness on matters which he changed at a later stage, but if that would be challenged by the Prosecution, then you would still have an opportunity to deal with those matters. That was the context in which, I think, I said we would not be generous but liberal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It wasn't related to that very narrow point. However, there was an issue raised as to policy of the state, and what I wanted to explore with him now is the contrast between saying there was a policy of the state on the one hand, and on other hand, going on national television on the 5th, expressing the exact opposite policy, and to explore how it came about and with whom, if anyone, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- presentation on national television was coordinated. And it goes directly to the issue of whether there was a policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you may put a few questions to the witness in relation to this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, did you discuss -- prior -- who did you have a conversation with prior to the -- your appearance on national television to discuss going on national television and issuing such an appeal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss that with anybody, anybody from the state authorities or county authorities or any other authorities. Whatever I said and whatever you heard me saying were my words, the words that I felt at the time, that I still feel, and that I will -- would feel tomorrow. I believe that I shared the joy of a number of Croatian people, as well as the citizens of Knin. I believe that I shared the joy of many citizens in the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, which were awaiting for the full -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I think -- I hope there is no misunderstanding between us. I didn't mean to suggest that somebody told you what to say. What I meant was, did you have a conversation with someone to say, I would like to go on TV and issue an appeal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Croatian TV approached me, and I, on my own, and I repeat, without anybody's prior instructions, provided the statement that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2981 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could I ask you one question. Did you write down the text before you spoke it on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you had written it down yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had written it down myself, like I do all of my texts. And since I always have stage fright before any appearance, just like have I now, I would not have been able to deliver the speech if I hadn't written it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is my last question, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could Exhibit P953 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it's just one follow-up question on the issue of housing in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's P953.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this is a report of the ECMM dated 9 October 1995, and this deals with, amongst other things, there was at paragraph 2, discusses: "Team Knin today had a meeting scheduled with the Housing Committee of the Knin mayor's office." Can you tell us what that might refer to? Did your office have a housing committee?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the previous question, I answered that the city of Knin had a housing commission, and president of that commission was my deputy for legal affairs, Mr. Slavko Djakovic. The housing commission and the decisions that it carried out were in the hands of Silvana Dumancic, who had a degree in law, and members of the commission were the employees of the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, and the Centre for Social Welfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph numbered 5, which is page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This paragraph discusses a meeting at the Tvik factory that the ECMM had and it discusses the role of the Tvik factory in returning economic development in the area. They had a discussion with the manager of the Tvik factory, and if we go down, it says towards the middle of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually in -- it says in paragraph B, there's a lack of skilled manpower. C is the big problem is the housing for the employees. And then towards the middle of the paragraph it says: "The possibility of Serbs to work on Tvik, demand for labour will not exceed 400, and a few Serbs will be employed. It is no problem to get unqualified employees, but Tvik is in big need of experts. Some of them will come from Zadar and even from Bosnia. He asks if the EU is willing to help them to organise a training course ... to get well-skilled personnel." And then the comment by the ECMM is: "Housing problem is paramount; nobody will come to work without this problem solved." Now, was there, Mr. Pasic, in your recollection and your understanding and knowledge of the working of the housing commission, a problem in bringing skilled labour into the area, because there was a lack of housing for people to come from outside of the Sector South to work within the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was no lack of housing. I believe that there are still a lot of empty apartments in Knin, even today. And if we're talking about labour force, professionals, then I would like to say that a lot of people who worked in companies such as Vijak had to leave Travnik, Bugojno, and other places, and they started working in the factory in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if -- if the Law on Temporary Take Over of Property had not been passed and if the Law on Socially Owned Flats had not been passed, would there still have been a lot of housing to employ skilled workers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it -- that question is both speculative, and with respect to the second law, there's no foundation that the witness is even aware of that law, let alone its substance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has testified that he is familiar with the work of the housing commission which was part of the town of Knin or mayor's office, depending on whether you believe the ECMM or how the witness has characterised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're actually asking is about what the effect of the legislation was on the existing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually just trying to clarify the witness's last answer. He says there was a lot of housing. Does he mean that in terms of just structures that are on the ground or does he mean they were available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness then first whether he could quantify that so that we know what we are talking about. Could you tell us if you said there was no lack of housing? Could you explain how many houses were there, for whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I couldn't give you the exact number of houses, but I believe that there were 4 to 5.000, and again, I'm not sure that there were 4 to 5.000 apartments. The Vijak factory had 3500 employees, and I assume that at its disposal it had at least 10 to 1200 housing units for its employees. And the other companies were no different, in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there were 4 to 500 apartments free to be occupied ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it is 4 to 5.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I thought -- 4 to 5.000 apartments in Knin alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that's correct. We were talking about 400 employees, as far as I could understand your question. 400 people could find employment in -- in the Vijak factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just clarify something for the Chamber, and I apologise if the Chamber is also aware of it. Vijak and Tvik, I believe, are synonymous. But perhaps the witness can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Vijak and Tvik, is that the same company or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Tvik is the abbreviation that stands for the factory for the production of nuts and bolts in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said there were 4 to 5.000 apartments in Knin available for housing. Is that ... That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And had there been a lot of construction, new apartments, after the Republic of Serbian Krajina had been established? You -- you lived in the area. Was there a lot of new apartments built over the last few years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I have to correct you. I -- since 1990, I have not lived in Knin. I was born there, but I resided and worked in Sibenik. During the Krajina authorities there were no jobs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just stop you there for a second. The reason why I'm asking is the following. I think that in the 1990 census there were some -- little bit over 3.000, perhaps 3.300 households. So therefore, the number of 4 to 5.000 apartments being available comes as a bit as a surprise to me. Therefore, I'm exploring with you whether this number is -- is based on what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was my assumption. First of all, the last census was in 1991, and, at that time, the city of Knin -- the city itself, had between 12.000 and 15.000 inhabitants. And I therefore assumed that given the fact that the JNA had its housing stock, the Croatian railways had its housing stock and so on and so forth, there was also the medical centre and hospital and all the others. That's what I based my assumptions on. I may have been mistaken, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, any further questions for the witness? I'm also looking at the clock. I -- of course, 15 minutes ago I thought we would be done in one or two minutes but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So did I, Mr. President. If I could just, then, have the break and I may be finished, and if I have anything, it will be two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the apologies to interpreters and all those who are assisting us. Mr. Pasic, we will first have a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since Mr. Misetic explored my topic, I will have no questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kay, I think, then, you have an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination, which --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- means ... Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: I want to ask something relating to your duties in Knin at the time that both you and Mr. Cermak were there. Were there any occasions when your duties overlapped, and, if the answer is yes, how was the problem dealt with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no overlapping. The commissioner's work did not overlap with the work of General Cermak, who was garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, how would you describe, then, the way your duties and his duties correlated.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties were connected with the work and programme of the ministry of the administration and justice of the Republic of Hrvatska, which means that my work fell within the purview of local administration and self-government. In our country the work of a city or a local self-government determined my authorities and the way I worked. As soon as I arrived in Knin, I had to create conditions for the life of people in the city of Knin. This primarily meant bringing electricity into town. There was no drinking water, and I also had to provide people with adequate accommodation, if they had expressed desire to settle in Knin, or those Croats who had been expelled in 1990 and 1991 and were accommodated in hotel villages in Solaris, Primosten and Vodica, or in the capital, Zagreb. I believe that some of the duties that I mentioned were carried out even better than in other areas liberated during Operation Storm, but it is not for me to talk about that. Within a very short period of time, we reconstructed and put into operation a nursery and a kindergarten for young families, and in the former building of a primary school, we restored the work of the Knin primary school because a lot of school children had returned to Knin. Soon after that, we also opened a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. If I could interrupt you, I think have you answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, continuing previous question what you respond just -- I'm a bit confused about your answer, because when I'm read your statement in -- given to Prosecution in 2002, and particularly page 4 and the paragraph which starts: "As far as I know, Cermak was there to assist the civil authorities." And then you mention: "He would direct me to organise the feeding of people which took place where Cermak had his office." We heard numerous evidence here that Cermak also is dealing with the same issues like you, electricity, water supply, and you told that there is no overlapping, or what kind of relations do you have between you and Cermak? It's still not clear for me.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Knin as the commissioner of the government of the Croatia, and I came from Sibenik, I have to tell you that there was a big difference between being the commissioner in exile in Knin, which means you were not in Knin, and the situation was even more difficult when we -- once we arrived in Knin. I repeat, Mr. Cermak had his powers, I had my powers. As far as General Cermak is concerned, I would like to say that the commissioner's office for Knin in exile did not have enough resources and staff to deal with the problems that occurred after Operation Storm. And let me say once again, that we enjoyed General Cermak's full help. Without him, many things would not have been done and resolved in a quality way, as I have already told to Madam Judge. Let me repeat, he had his powers, I had my powers, and our cooperation and mutual assistance was at a very high level, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But did he issue some instructions to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no instructions were given, either in a written or verbal form. We discussed things and that's how we decided how to do things. He never issued me with any written or oral instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that your office didn't have sufficient amount of finances and resources. Could you please tell me who -- how much resources was at Cermak's disposal? You mentioned here in your testimony yesterday that villages were supplied by generators, by televisions. And so where he got this stuff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was speaking about my resources, I did not talk about money but about human resources that the commissioner's office had at its disposal at the time. I didn't have any problems with funding, because the funds from the Ministry of Finance were delivered on time, even before Operation Storm when we were working in exile, and later on, the monies went through Zadar and Knin county and they reached us through them. How Mr. Cermak's office was funded, I don't know. I never inquired and it was not up to me to inquire. As far as your question is concerned, and your curiosity about televisions, after Operation Storm, many company delegates, representatives and individuals arrived in Knin. They brought donations. They brought TV sets, food, and I believe that those donations -- and to me personally, I received financial donation from Australia for the first marriage in Knin, actually there were two marriages that took place at the same time so I had to split that donation between two -- two couples who got married at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I have a few questions for you as well. First, in relation to one of your previous answers, could you give me a name of the company that would provide television sets to your office or the office of Mr. Cermak, which you then distributed in the Oton village?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the company in question was Frotea. The TV sets were donated by the representative of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce of the then Croatian republic Herceg-Bosna. I believe that his name was Jago Lasic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any documents in which they are offered, a letter sent, Here, you've got five or ten television sets. Is there any documentary evidence which would support your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing. At that time donations just arrived. People would, for example, come to my office or to Mr. Cermak's office with donations. Later on, we tried to record those donations, which were then in a different form, and we tried to distribute those donations through the office of the Croatian Red Cross that was in charge of that. Let me just tell that you in the vicinity of the Croatian Army hall, the municipality of Donja Stubica, built a house, one of the only two that were shelled in the city of Knin. There's no written document to that effect, no written document to show that the house was the result of a donation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these television sets, were they delivered at your office or Mr. Cermak's office, before you took them to Oton village?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were brought to Mr. Cermak. But we carried them there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you learn which firm supplied these television sets?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, some of those people who had donated some gifts, after the meeting with Mr. Cermak, visited me. They paid me a visit in my office, the office of the commissioner's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And these were all new television sets?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You believe so. What could create any doubt?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were packed in cardboard boxes. Well, I didn't really inspect them, to be absolutely sure that they were new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said they gave the impression that were in the original carton boxes. Moving to a totally different subject. Upon arrival here in The Hague you explained to the Cermak Defence that after reviewing your statements over a couple of days, you would like to make changes. How long did that meeting take, approximately, in which you informed the Cermak Defence about the changes you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in The Hague, in my statement provided to the investigator, I did not make any changes concerning General Cermak. The changes that I made concerned other things and matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my question was: How long the meeting in which you expressed your wish to make these changes lasted.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour or so, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you go through your statements? Did you go through it page by page, or had you prepared a list of changes? What happened during this one-hour meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already before that, I had already made up my mind as to what parts of the statement needed to be changed, and I spontaneously provided different answers, with the professional help of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Had you put them on paper already, what the real answers should be, for yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
