utterances.text: So you had prepared a document for yourself, on the basis of which you informed the Cermak Defence about your wish to make some changes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you still have that document in your possession?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. Once we made the changes, I received the new text, and I signed every single page personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened with the document you had prepared? Did you give it to the Cermak Defence, or did you ...

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tore it up, and -- well, I would feel embarrassed to actually have to tell you where I put it, what I did with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if there's any reason why you wouldn't say it in an open session, then, of course, in order to protect your privacy, we could turn into private session. But I would like to know where -- what happened to that document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a document. It was a piece of paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which I flushed down the toilet. I did not want that piece of paper to be abused, either by me or by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the risk of abuse of that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- I didn't feel any imminent risk. I just didn't want anybody else but me being in a position to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And all the papers that I have now, I will store them out of anybody's reach, because I don't want anybody to either read them or have access to them, for any reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, on that piece of paper, did you work on the basis of paragraphs of your statement? Could you tell us what you wrote down? And let me just go back to one of your previous answers. You told me that you had put on paper already what the real answers should be. Did you write that down in your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do it any other way. I don't use computers, printers, or anything of the sort, and I did not have any equipment at my disposal. As I prepared for work and certain activities, I would write down several drafts of speeches or plans for activities, and then I would work further on them, as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did I understand your previous answer well, that you -- let me just ... Had you formulated the answers you considered correct on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you copy, first, the old answers, and then add what the true answers would be; or did you just make a paragraph reference and then add what the new text should be? Could you tell us which way you did that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my papers, I checked for things that were not correct, and I based my corrections on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then you put the right answers written out on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was that one sheet, several sheets; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several sheets. I couldn't put all the seven corrections on one sheet. And, as I told you already, I change things several times round before I am happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was any change made to what you had written down and what we finally found in this document that was made on this Tuesday, the -- or did the Cermak Defence copy all of your answers; or did you refine the formulation? Were there any changes to what you had put on paper?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written text of the answers was my language, my formulations. Perhaps there may have been certain additions from the professional side, by the team of attorneys. In any case, they did not touch upon my right to have this or that type of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said the meeting lasted only one hour -- or approximately one hour, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you then read the new answers to them, or did you, at any moment, give them a copy of what you had prepared?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read them, and then, together with them, we were trying to find the right formulation so as to keep the answer in line with what it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you write them down in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was an interpreter present during that meeting on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did he, on the spot, translate your language into English; or did he, at any moment, had this piece of paper so as to put it in proper English on what was later presented to us as your additional statement or at least the corrections?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was present as the interpreter interpreted from Croatian into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I change subjects again. You told us about -- that you had a conversation in which it was said that it would not be good if President Tudjman would see the -- the burning. Did you ever consider that, if Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, would visit the area, that if there would have been smoke, that the international community, ambassadors, other high officials, would say to him, Well, you've seen it yourself. Was that of any concern to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consider the possibility that the president or someone else could see smoke. I don't know whether the president was fed correct information from the field or not. I can't say that. I did not send in reports. Someone else probably did, but I can't know what sort of reports reached the president. However, I am certain that the president of the Republic would not have been happy with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have misunderstood my question. You -- the first part of your answer was: "I didn't consider the possibility that the president or someone else could see smoke." Do I have to understand your testimony to be that, on this -- I think it was the 26th of August, that travelling by train through the area would not -- you wouldn't see any smoke of houses that were or had been burning before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you discussed that it would not be good and that the burning should stop. Again, if you couldn't see any smoke, what was your -- why would you consider it not to be good to see smoke if there was no smoke to be seen at all? That's at least what you expected.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the translation does not correspond to ... maybe I would change it again. In my conversation with Mr. Cermak, I may have used the words "the president would not have been glad," but I thought it might have been good, irrespective of the president and other officials who accompanied him on the liberty train, to have that stopped. In that case, I thought that it would be good that as of now, not as of the president's arrival, that there be any other burning of property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the gist, then, of your conversation was that it would not be good if there would be any further burning, apart from that the president would not have been in a position to see any smoke at all.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Change subjects again. I think some questions were put to you in relation to a hundred Serbs having returned to Knin, and we are at the end of October when this would have happened. And you told us that at least one group returned, organised, arriving in a bus. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how many Serbs approximately were living in Knin, even before the war started?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the census from 1991, in Knin, that is to say, the area of the former Knin municipality, there lived some 38 or 39.000 Serbs. The percentage it amounted to was 89, 8, some per cent were Croats, and three and a half, or 3 per cent, were of those who did not declare their ethnicity or declare themselves Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the hundred Serbs that had returned by the end of October, were you referring to the town of Knin only or were you referring to the Knin municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some arrived in the town of Knin; whereas, others went to some rural parts further from Knin. That is to say, to the villages where they had left from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when this was discussed, I got the impression that - but please correct me when I'm wrong - that you considered this, well, an achievement, a hundred Serbs having returned, something noteworthy. Is that a misapprehension of what you meant to say, or ...

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not misunderstand. The traces of war were still felt, and persons had to express their wish to return. Some of them may have felt fear, but, later on -- well, you know how it is. When one family returns to a village and then they let others know that there were no problems, then they began returning more frequently. If I may, you are referring to this figure of 100. If I said there were some 3.000 Croats, only 250 out of that total number of Croats saw the beginning of the operation in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, 100 out of close to a 40.000 is one-quarter of 1 per cent. Did you consider that, at that time, to be an achievement which would support that the return of Serbs was going well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it is an inherent right of every person to live where they want to. What I can say is that even thought there are conditions in place for their return now, people still did not return. They found other means of living, some of them remained in the Republic of Serbia, but, unfortunately, most of the population of Knin is not in Serbia but in Canada, Australia, and America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You referred to -- that the conditions are in place for return but people still did not return. Could you give us a figure as to how many of those 38 to 40.000 you mentioned before have now returned today? If you know. If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I do take part in the meetings of the Serb National Council at which it is mentioned that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, from Operation Storm to date, some 112 to 115.000 people returned. In my estimate, most of them returned to the area of the former Knin municipality, because most was -- the most was done there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any statistics or figures on that? Because, if 40.000 left, it may be -- it may be a need of some further explanation if you say that 112 to 115.000 people returned. Then, apparently, we're talking about different groups or different places, different areas. Do you have any statistics on specifically Knin area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. This figure covers the entire Republic of Croatia after Operations Flash and Storm. I think the return in greatest number, in terms of Serbs, was in the area around Knin and the town itself, because that is where the most was done in the process of reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to the witness? Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, several matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can we deal, first of all, with the changes that made to your Prosecution statement, and I want to ask you questions about that arising from His Honour Judge Orie's questions. Firstly, did you tell the Cermak Defence which paragraphs, which parts of the statement you wanted to change?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it ever suggested to you by any member of the Cermak Defence team that you should ever change any part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are quite leading questions, and in the circumstances, perhaps they should be put in a more open-ended way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can't think of any other way of putting the question. It's not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- however, Mr. Kay, it's -- if, in my questions, there was any such suggestion included, and I think it was not, but then that certainly was not what I intended to discuss with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I don't know what the Bench is thinking, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's the reason why I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was mainly focussing on prepared new text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I will direct my questions to that, given Your Honour'S guidance on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it -- did you point out which parts of the statement needed to be changed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I alone, without any influence, decided which changes need to be made, and in keeping with that, I suggested the right answers, or the replacement that should take place, due to the change I wished to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was what you told the Cermak Defence written down by a member of their team at the time, as you spoke?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you speak in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as a result of what you said, was a document typed up the same day that was put to you for your approval?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you read that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did it reflect what you had told the Cermak Defence at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then did you sign that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just moving on to some other matters, in answer to Her Honour Judge Gwaunza, you said that you had to create the conditions for life of electricity, drinking water, accommodation. Now, taking, first of all, electricity, did General Cermak have any role to play in relation to the connection of the electricity for Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak was not in charge of re-establishing the water supply, electricity supply, soup kitchens or some other elements required for the functioning of the town of Knin. However, I felt the need, or I realised that, with my team, we were not able to overcome the obstacles before us. It is then that I asked General Cermak to help me. He did so, to the best of his ability, to deal with those problems in Knin. I can tell that you in a very short period of time, the town of Knin had potable water and most of the settlements near Knin began receiving electricity. Where there were greater distances involved and where there was more destruction, General Cermak personally, in my village, it may have been because of me perhaps, brought a generator, where the people who received the TV sets I mentioned could watch them. That generator enabled the use of electricity for the inhabitants, by the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, if we can take this in stages. The electricity, did Knin have to be reconnected to the electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The town of Knin did not have electricity supply. I believe the commander of the Military District and the military garrison --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Garrison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As the witness says, had their own generators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just correcting there a translation error that we've had several -- several times on the word "garrison."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, that is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The electricity, then, was connected by the garrison. Was that work that you were able to do with your staff or did it require a different competence to do that work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the employees of the Croatian electricity supply company, and in particular the Commission of the Republic of Croatia, were insufficiently equipped to be able to deal with the problems which cropped up after the Operation Storm in Knin. We asked to be helped --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And where did that help come from? Who helped you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to deal with the situation, the Croatian electrical company sent teams from Split and Zadar. They also sent in teams to re-establish the telephone network. The area of Knin was in the territory of the Zadar department. Some people also arrived from the postal centres in Split and Sibenik, and I believe much was done in order to resolve the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to those works, what did the garrison do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison, although I didn't mention it, probably had to provide food and accommodation for those people. But I forgot to mention, and I don't know whether I was asked about that, that the public utility company of the town of Knin had to become operational right after Operation Storm, and we managed to do that. Irrespective of the fact that I was the governmental commissioner, I was not a familiar face in that area, and I relied on the position and reputation of Mr. Cermak to assist me. He did so, by virtue of his connections, I presume from Zagreb, where he hails from, brought in a public utility team from Zagreb. They cleaned the streets round the clock. Thus, clearing the town of Knin of any debris or leftover garbage which had not been taken away during the previous -- during the rule of the previous authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that work necessary to normalise life in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it not been for the clean-up team, which dealt with Knin itself, I believe, in a very short time, the situation would have become unbearable. People could not live or return to Knin. There probably would have been an outbreak or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning now to the drinking water, in relation to restoring drinking water to Knin and the area, are you able to say what work the garrison did, in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison -- I didn't know some of the people who had worked there before, but the garrison managed to locate an expert team. Knin is supplied with water rather specifically from a source called Vrelo. It's a source of water, and perhaps all that was necessary was to reconnect the pumps and then water began flowing. I think there was a certain Cacic, who was the person who had worked previously with that equipment, who was brought in from Zagreb in order to deal with the water supply of Knin as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who was bringing in the -- the person from Zagreb to deal with the water supply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know who brought him in. But I think that, during a meeting, some mention was made of a person who would be an expert to deal with it, and I believe it was on the suggestion of the garrison that he was brought in from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mention funds and donations. What sort of things were being donated by others to Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about donations I can say that donations varied. I have already told you that a man came to me, he was the mayor of Donja Stubica, he brought some workmen and they restored a house -- the house belonged to Mr. Jakovljevic. Actually, there were three owners. One of them was Sota Jakovljevic [phoen]. They did it in a very short time. Then there was this donation of TV sets. There were also building materials that were donated. But I have to say that when a soup kitchen was opened to feed those who were not able to provide for themselves, it was moved from the place where it stood originally to the premises of the former Balkan restaurant, and it received donations in food. I must again point out that some of the people that donated things, I didn't know. I have to tell you that a man came and he was the owner of a meat processing factory. His name was either Jakopec or Jakopec, I don't know exactly. And owing to his previous acquaintance with Mr. Cermak and the reputation that Mr. Cermak enjoyed, because of Mr. Cermak and because of people who needed help, a very impressive donation arrived, consisting of dry cured meats and cold cuts and fresh meat as well. According it my estimate, the soup kitchen, which provided a daily supply of some 300 meals, was well supplied with meat products and fresh meat that lasted for over ten days. Likewise, I have to say that this was a joint agreement with General Cermak, because we ceded a former bakery shop to a man who had returned to the city of Knin. His name was Teskera. He supplied the soup kitchen with a month's worth supply of bread for all those who benefited from the services of the soup kitchen. I really can't remember all the other donations at the moment. There may have been some donations that were not even needed at the time, some wicker chairs or garden furniture, but I must tell you that those donations were presented to either Mr. Cermak or myself. We did not distribute the goods according to needs. If the donations consisted of food, clothes and footwear, then we would call the secretary of the Red Cross office, whose name was Tanja Grgic, because the Red Cross, I must admit, was really well organised, very mobile, and with the assistance of international humanitarian organisations it was fully equipped to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm wondering whether we have not reached a level of detail which might not assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's a document I would like you to look at. It is 65 ter 2D00314. And, Mr. Pasic, if you can look at the screen there to your right at a document dated the 8th of August, from the garrison. Signed by Mr. Cermak. Sent to Zadar-Knin county, Orlovic donation, care of Mr. Kumana. Do you know a Mr. Kumana at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kuman, while I was the commissioner of the Republic of Croatia for Knin, was -- held the same duty for Benkovac. And when this document was drafted or, rather, when this request was drafted, I believe that he was the head of the prefect's office for reconstruction of development. I'm not sure about that. But I know that he was a county official and that he was the head of one of the county offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you see the content of this application, you see that it's due to the normalisation of work and return of civilians to the town of Knin, "I hereby ask you to donate one power generator from the Orlovic donation" and signed by General Cermak. First of all, did you know about this request for a donation by General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know at the time whether the Orlovic donation in fact gave a generator to the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the generator went to Oton Bender, where it was installed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is dated the 8th of August, 1995. Would that have been a generator that went to Oton Bender on that date?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 8th of August, that's the date of the application. And when the application was dealt with and when the generator went up there, I don't know. I can't be -- I can't be sure of that. However, I believe that some time lapsed, before the generator arrived in Knin and dispatched to the place where it would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this was re-examination, although we didn't have the usual sequence of examination of the witness. Therefore, without now a liberal approach anymore, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will keep it strictly to the questions from the Bench, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you answered some questions from the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie - at page 45, lines 3 to 6, for the benefit of the parties - and this was when you were asked about donations of television sets. And you specifically referenced that this came from a man named Jago Lasic, who - if I can just find the line - was chairman of commerce -- or, sorry. Croatian Chamber of Commerce of the then Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Then you were asked by the Presiding Judge: Are you aware of any documents in which they are offered, a letter sent, Here you've got five or ten television sets. Now, I would like to show you a video concerning -- which is related to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, play 65 ter 1D2982.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The last four years in Knin can be characterised as years of idleness and disorder. But this for some time [indiscernible], says Petar Pasic, the commissioner of the government of the Republic of Croatia for Knin. Today the president of the Chamber of Commerce of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia, Mr. Jago Lasic, has promised to provide his full assistance in the realisation of this goal. And together with his associates and several companies from Herceg-Bosnia, he visited this town today. This time, aside from their promise of future cooperation, they also brought aid to Zvonimir Grad [phoen] in the value of approximately 1.850.000 kuna and two computers as a gift to the local hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, that meeting on the 28th of August, is that the meeting with Mr. Lasic to which you were referring in answer to the Presiding Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were there any other meetings with Mr. Lasic in Knin, other than the one on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any others. But I know that he brought a number of people who was his associates on his visit to Knin. I believe there was the representative of a company whose name was Frotea or something like that. I can't remember after 15 years. I know that there were a lot of people, that they all promised assistance and that they did, indeed, follow through and sent donations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the video it's referenced that Mr. Lasic and the group that came with him from Herceg-Bosna brought aid in the value of approximately 1.850.000 kuna. Can you describe for us the form in which that -- the form which that aid took; in other words, was it 1.850.000 in value of goods, or was it cash?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cash, you mean? I -- I believe that there was no cash involved. I believe that the donation that arrived from the then leadership of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce of Herceg-Bosna, as far as I know, was sent to the Knin hospital, which already, at the time, had already started working, and I assumed that the chief administrator of the Knin hospital, Mr. Biskovic, had taken over the donation, whatever it was. I believe that he was the one who took the donation over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But were the televisions that you referred to in your answers to Judge Orie, were the televisions part of this donation that's referenced there of 1.850.000 kuna?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2982 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Any further questions on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Pasic, where was this aid delivered, as far as you remember? If you know. The goods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, judging by the -- the image of the event by -- judging by the pictures, I believe that the meeting was held on the premises of the government of the Republic of Croatia. I believe that it was in my office, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's where the goods were delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Save for the TV sets and the -- the monitors -- I don't know what to call them. I believe that one part of the donation actually ended up with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that Mr. Lasic had brought a number of people, economists from the area, executives and businessmen. I believe that they brought a lot of towels, clothing items that had been donated by a company whose name is Frotea, as I've already told you already. And I believe that we immediately involved the Croatian Red Cross, that immediately embarked on the distribution of those donated goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Goods were immediately distributed then, upon receipt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I believe so. I can't see that on the screen, but I believe that, when it comes to donations, Mr. Curko was also present at the meeting. He was the head of the welfare centre, and I believe that Mrs. Tanja Grgic, from the Croatian Red Cross, was also present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was no list of goods in this amount of 1.850.000 kuna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A reference is made to the value as being 1.850.000 kuna. I can't really tell you whether that amount is correct. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether the amount was correct. I asked you whether there was list of goods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if I can ask you, you were asked some questions about the numbers of Serbs that had returned to Knin by the end of October 1995. How many Croats who are from the Knin municipality - in other words, Croats from the Knin municipality in 1991 or before - how many of them had returned to the Knin municipality by end of October 1995? By "return," I mean returned to live.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government's recommendation was first to accommodate Croats who were, at the time, accommodated in hotels. There were some 1.261 citizens of Kijevo, they were all Croats but one. At the time they were accommodated in the bungalows of Resnik or Trogir or somewhere in that area. And they immediately expressed -- expressed a desire to leave the tourist complex and they returned. They had previously owned houses, and their village was razed to the ground, and they expressed a wish before the housing commission to be accommodated in the former state-owned apartments and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- those Croats who had expressed their desire to return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please focus on the question. How many of the Croats that had lived before the war started in 1991 had returned by the end of October to Knin. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting at this stage but I just needed to double-check. These questions arose initially from an ECMM report of the 27th of October P822, and in which this witness reports that a figure, if he is going to asked about it now, perhaps he should be shown that document. He refers both to the hundred Serbs and to the numbers of Croats and from -- from where they stem or are from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it's suggested that you ... let's try to finish within the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can we -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have Exhibit D822.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe it is P822.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: P, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, you'll see in this document that it reports that most Croats who lived in Knin before 1991 had returned, and that that statement is attributed to you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that -- did you say that at the end of October 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that I said this. I know the exact number of Croats, segregated by places. It says there were five and a half thousand people who remained ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I think what it says, Mr. Pasic, is that there were 1300 who were from Knin and there are another 5.500 who are in Knin at that moment but who have roots elsewhere. Was that something that you had said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I have already told that you a large number of Croats arrived from Banja Luka, they arrived from Travnik. They arrived from Bugojno. And the reason for their arrival, as I was told, they told me themselves, was the fact that they could not live together with the Muslims, and that's why they wanted to return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, my question is this. First, just by way of background and I don't know if this is in your statement. I don't think it is. After you were the commissioner for Knin until March of 1996, you continued to be the commissioner for which municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is wrong. It was not the 4th of September but the 9th of September. Actually the 9th of April, 1996, I was removed from the position of the commissioner of the government of the Republic of Croatia, but on the same day I was appointed a commissioner of the Republic of Croatia for the municipalities of Civljane, Biskupija, Kistanje, and Ervenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that position, until when?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held that position until the 16th of January, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we are drifting far away from what apparently what was raised by my questions. I asked for the appreciation of a number the witness gave at the time. Now you asked him how many Croats had returned. We find in this document reported that the witness would have said approximately 1300, and practically all of the Croats. It is not a core issue of this case. I'm not saying it's irrelevant, but it's not a core issue in this case. The witness said that this is what he said, and now we're exploring his previous positions. Either one or two focussed questions on the matter. Otherwise, we'll end up far from what I raised and which was not primarily focussing on figures and numbers. But, rather, about an appreciation by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just have a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, since it's not a core issue, then I will not pursue the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it is, I didn't hear you say it's not. But it's certainly a matter which has some relevance and has been dealt with over in a considerable way. But if it is not, I expressed as my view that, although there is relevance to the issue, it's not a core issue, and by leaving that, if it is not a core issue, then we'll hear from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reason I qualified that way, Mr. President, is precisely because, as can you appreciate in my position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may give it -- you gave -- may give it a higher level of relevance than you could understand from my words and what is the core is still, of course, a concept which is not precisely defined. Mr. Pasic - I'm looking at the parties - this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered, for a few days, all the questions that were put to by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. By your leave, I wish to say that I hope you will believe everything what I said and what I commented about concerning my interview and previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can understand that you have that hope. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza is not available for a very short moment. The other Judges considered it in the interests of justice to proceed, and it's mainly a procedural matter which I would like to deal with in private session. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Cipci, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I would just like to clear up one housekeeping matter which was the pages of the suspect interview. I've had a chance to look at more carefully and if the Chamber is inclined to admit that exhibit, which is D1719, in our submission, the six prior pages, so starting at page 57 of that interview, provides the appropriate context, in particular, for the statement of the investigator, where it says, "It seems from what you are saying." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now pages and videos, may I take it that you want to have this portion of the video then added as well and not just the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's up to Your Honours. I don't -- I don't think the video is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, for the context, we could just do with the transcript, Mr. Misetic, would that meet any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, Mr. President, take a look at the full transcript. I don't have it with me here in court. I just have the selection and I will get back to the Chamber in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the ball is on your side now again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, this -- there were two reasons why it was marked for identification. The Chamber will still have to consider the relevance, whether that's a matter of admissibility or whether it's a matter of weight, as suggested by Ms. Gustafson. I see now three counsel at the side of the Prosecution. Who will be in charge of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. De Landri will take the next witness. Yes, that's on the record then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Cipci, could you please remain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- standing, yes. Mr. Cipci, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. And I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration. If you remain standing when giving that -- yes, the microphone will catch your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cipci.

utterances.speaker: MS. DE LANDRI
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The screen reflects that we're still in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Then -- I think in the beginning of the -- I do not see that on other screens.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have different --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption. I can confirm we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But our screens still puts us in private or closed session. No, it's -- as a matter of fact, it's the ELMO screen which gives closed session but the video screen is, at this moment, fully public, and that's the one that is broadcasted. Mr. Kay, please proceed. You will first -- Mr. Cipci, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, don't worry about the microphones. They're extremely powerful and they will pick up your voice when you speak. Mr. Cipci, is it correct that you made a statement to the Defence for this case, dated the 3rd of September, 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: It is correct that I made that statement, which I also signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have 2D00740, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cipci, on the right-hand screen you will see in a moment a copy of that statement in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if the signature could be shown at the foot of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that there that document, Mr. Cipci, as being the record of interview signed for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature and the cover page of my statement. It is precisely the statement I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I know you have a copy of it in front of you in a plastic folder. Don't worry about that. That's just a copy and we'll all be looking at the one on the screen. If you need to refer to that paper copy, just ask us for permission to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can go to the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise there your signature next to the date of the 3rd of September, 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd of September, 2009, and the signature is indeed mine. I wrote both the date and I affixed the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we know that your signature is on each page in between. Did you read through this statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Certainly. First I read it and then I signed each page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to paragraph 13, which is on page 5 in the English, line 23. So page 5, line 23, in the English.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can have that on the screen in front of you in Croatian, on the right-hand side. And we see a sentence containing: "100 policemen." In English it reads: "He came to Knin with his policemen with the first contingent of 100 policemen. Mr. Sikrica was formally responsible to Mr. Romanic and he received orders from him." Is it correct that you want to make a correction, in relation to that sentence?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] It is correct that I want to make a small correction in this sentence. On the 5th, in the afternoon, the first contingent of 100 policemen was accompanied by Mr. Milkovic who remained there only for a few days and then he was replaced by Mr. Sikrica. I mention Mr. Sikrica because he spent a longer period of time being in charge of that unit, that is why I mentioned Sikrica rather than Maljkovic. But in the course of the first few days and the first afternoon, it was Mr. Maljkovic who was with the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's spelt M-a-l-j-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: [In English] Not. [Interpretation] Not quite. It should be M-a-i-l-j. [In English] L and g together. Then k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mailjkovic. And it's not just a plain C but it is actually Ch in Croatian. We have a two different versions of it. They come with a diacritic and then you would have the right last name. But, in any case, it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've got that piece of information. So taking into account that corrections that you have now made before the Court on that matter in paragraph 13, is everything that you have said in this statement, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: What I stated, I personally assume that everything is correct. However, the truth and a lie are very subjective categories, and what I am claiming at this moment or what I will claim as opposed to what I claimed in the past, I can only say, at the moment, when I stated that, I was convinced that I was telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I were to ask you today the same questions that you were asked previously, would the information in this statement reflect and be the same as the answers that you have given to the statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: If you were to ask me the identical questions, I would answer them in the identical way. The only difference with regard to my statement that I provided on the 3rd is what I stated at -- previously, with regards to the family names of those who left for Knin on the 5th. So it wasn't Mr. Sikrica but Mr. Mailjkovic. And that's the only change that I would made to the answers that I would provide and they would be the same as back then, when you asked me all those questions and the answers became my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I noticed that you have a natural inclination of giving rather long answers. This matter, if would you have said, I would give the same answers with the correction I just made, would have sufficient for us to understand fully what meant. I would invite you to focus very much and to give brief answers. If any further details are relevant, Mr. Kay will certainly ask you for those details. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the witness, having made that statement, I request that this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was already submitted that there would be no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. DE LANDRI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the statement of Mr. Cipci would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1723 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to this statement, Your Honour, I want to point out a matter which is probably on the record already, but so it's on the trial record. And that concerns paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have no need to worry about this, Mr. Cipci, it's a matter of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A document was referred to by an internal reference number, OBR 416, that's in fact Exhibit D495, Your Honour, and that correction was notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber received a notification to that extent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Your Honour, also in the English version, a sentence had not been typed in. The full version has been uploaded so that paragraph 30 fully reflects what was said in the Croatian original that the witness signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the counsel for the Prosecution. I take it that that is agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DE LANDRI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, if we could just look at a part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm turning now, Your Honour, to paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 23, where you deal with a matter concerning passes that were issued by Mr. Cermak. And you've been shown, when you made your statement, a number of documents that are reflected in the statements, numbers -- Exhibits D497, 498, 494, and Exhibit D495, and Exhibit D496.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Exhibit D496, if that could be put on to the screen, please, so that Mr. Cipci can look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement, you refer to the re-establishment of the Split-Knin train line and a number of people wanting to travel. And you can see on the document in front of you that it is from the Split-Dalmatia police administration, dated the 15th of August, 1995, and you can see your name at the end of the document, and that it is sent to Operative Action Povratak. And it is sent to the Ministry of Interior with the subject: Visits and administration [sic] to the liberated areas. First of all, Mr. Cipci, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was it a document sent by you to your Ministry of Interior in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: Yes. To the office for return. That was an office within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the office for return, if could you just briefly inform the Court what the nature of that particular office was, what it was concerned with.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: The office was set up within the Ministry of the Interior and it was headed by the Assistant Minister Josko Moric. It was supposed to deal with all sorts of communications in the area and evaluate whether all the conditions were in place to abolish passes which were the only relevant documents that allowed people to enter the liberated area. In other words, they oversaw the restoration of normal life in the area, as well as all the other tasks and duties given to them by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see from the content of this letter, that you were saying you were being pressured by citizens and displaced persons wishing to visit the liberated areas, and that the railroad line was restored and that the railroad line was to transport citizens for free within the next ten days, and that there is enormous pressure at check-points, because citizens feel they can travel without any problem. And you asked: "Please give us urgent directions how to" -- "as to how we should act in this newly developed situation." Can you briefly describe to the Court, then, the problem that you were experiencing at this time when you wrote this letter and sent it to the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: It was not just the problem of people who previously resided in the area and who enjoyed the status of returnees. There was a great deal of interest among other citizens from the territory of my police administration, which was the county of Split and Dalmatia, to move into that area that had been occupied for years. They wanted to settle in Knin, to arrive in Knin by way of providing contribution to the liberation of the area, and that's why there was lot of pressure from -- on the police administration, the railway administration, because I know it for a fact that all those who wanted to get on the train couldn't. There were too many people who wanted to go to Knin. That's why I sought instructions, because the civilians could pass through my check-points only with passes signed by myself. I certainly could not issue thousands of passes, because I had very strict criteria as to who could go to the liberated areas at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I had one more question to ask on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see handwritten on it: "Call the Split-Dalmatia police administration and say that Cermak will annul the passes today." And do you know what that handwritten reference concerns?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this and what that refers to. As far as I know, Mr. Cermak, based on the previous agreements in the ministry prior to the beginning of Operation Storm, Mr. Cermak could not issue passes for my area and for my check-points and he also, by the same token, could not abolish them. At the end of the day, I received information from the ministry that passes would no longer be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that deals with that matter. Your Honour, there's further questions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cipci, we have to adjourn for the day. You have been with us only for a very short moment, but tomorrow further questions will be there for you to answer. But I'd like, first of all, to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether the evidence already given today, or the evidence still to be given tomorrow. So refrain from any conversations on that matter, or any communications. We will adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, because we will resume on the 14th of October, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
